medical.title: Adenotonsillectomy tied to increase in respiratory tract infections in children
medical.summary: Adenotonsillectomy (ATE) is associated with increased odds of hospital visits due to upper and lower respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in children, according to a study published online July 31 in the Journal of Rhinology.

medical.title: Higher vitamin B12 levels in both parents associated with a lower risk of birth defects
medical.summary: A prospective cohort study quantifying the associations of parental vitamin B12 and red blood cell (RBC) folate with birth defects found that higher parental vitamin B12 before conception and higher maternal RBC folate concentrations after conception were associated with lower birth defect risk.

medical.title: Estimated glucose disposal rate inversely linked to benign prostatic hyperplasia
medical.summary: There is a negative link between estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men, according to a study published online Aug. 25 in The Aging Male.

medical.title: Lab-grown nerves match human sensory signal speeds, enabling tests of myelin repair
medical.summary: Rice University and collaborators in Switzerland have developed a platform to grow human-derived nerve cells and Schwann cells, supporting cells that form a protective coating called myelin around nerve fibers. This platform enables the formation of functional myelin in a three-dimensional, lab-grown environment. Researchers confirmed that it worked by measuring an increase in the speed of electrical signals traveling across networks of connected nerve cells.

medical.title: Semen facilitates infection with mpox virus, study shows
medical.summary: The mpox virus used to be transmitted predominantly from animals to humans. In recent years, however, new virus variants have become increasingly capable of spreading from person to person. Researchers at Goethe University and Universitätsmedizin Frankfurt have now found that seminal fluid facilitates the uptake of the mpox virus into cells. Their study is published in the journal Emerging Microbes & Infections.

medical.title: Updated guideline issued on migraine prevention medications for adults
medical.summary: To help clinicians determine which medications may be most effective at preventing migraine in adults, the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and American Headache Society (AHS) have issued a joint practice guideline update with evidence-based recommendations, published in Neurology, and Headache. This update to the AAN and AHS 2012 guideline is endorsed by the American Academy of Family Physicians.

medical.title: Tumor 'floor plans' may predict immunotherapy response better than current biomarkers
medical.summary: Spatial transcriptomics is a powerful tool for creating a detailed map of not just how genes are expressed in a piece of tissue, but also where genetic activity takes place in different cells and locations within the tissue. This is especially valuable for studying tumors, which each have their own unique microenvironment that affects how they behave.

medical.title: 2011 to 2021 saw heart failure-related hospitalization rise in CKD
medical.summary: For patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), rates of heart failure-related hospitalization increased from 2011 to 2021, according to a study published in the September issue of Kidney International Reports.

medical.title: Damaged red blood cells can trigger inflammation
medical.summary: When red blood cells break down, they release heme, a component of hemoglobin that can contribute to inflammation and damage tissues and blood vessels. Researchers at Lund University have identified a mechanism by which heme activates an inflammatory reaction in the blood. They also were able to block this pathway in experimental models. The findings could have implications for diseases and conditions involving extensive breakdown of red blood cells, including hemolytic uremic syndrome and malaria.

medical.title: New AI method can support real-time management of infectious diseases
medical.summary: For the past 25 years, one discipline has been revolutionizing epidemiology: phylodynamics. By using genetic sequences, scientists can study how pathogens evolve. Thanks to mathematics, these data can be coherently organized into phylogenetic trees, with each branch representing a chain of transmission and each leaf representing an individual infection.

medical.title: Health systems joining efforts to reduce homelessness
medical.summary: From developing housing to deploying mobile medical units, most of the nation's large health systems are investing in efforts to alleviate homelessness—and, in turn, reduce emergency care costs, new Cornell research finds.

medical.title: Long-term intensive blood-pressure control reduces dementia risk, community-led trial finds
medical.summary: In a community-based trial in rural China, an intensive blood pressure-lowering intervention reduced the incidence of dementia compared with usual care, according to results from the China Rural Hypertension Control Program presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

medical.title: Poor diet may worsen genetic causes of male infertility, study finds
medical.summary: Lifestyle factors can worsen the effects of genetic causes of male infertility, finds new research that could help explain why men carrying similar genetic mutations often experience different levels of fertility impairment.

medical.title: Evidence often falls short in neuroscience reports of sex-dependent effects, analysis finds
medical.summary: Studies in the behavioral and brain sciences reporting a major sex-dependent effect—that a drug, treatment or other intervention is more effective in one sex than another—are supported by appropriate evidence less than 25% of the time, an analysis finds.

medical.title: Mouth ulcers: Why have I got them and how can I get rid of them?
medical.summary: If you've ever had a mouth ulcer, you'll know how much a tiny sore can take over your day. These small, painful patches that suddenly appear inside your mouth make eating, drinking and even talking surprisingly uncomfortable.

medical.title: TAVI-first strategy noninferior to a PCI-first strategy in patients with severe aortic stenosis and concomitant CAD
medical.summary: A TAVI-first strategy was noninferior to a PCI-first strategy after one year's follow-up, according to results presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

medical.title: Four disease profiles reveal uneven benefits from lifestyle programs after age 70
medical.summary: Older adults living with several chronic diseases, a condition known as multimorbidity, may respond differently to interventions aimed at preventing disability, depending on the combination of diseases they have. A new study, published in Nature Aging and led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Rome, suggests that looking at patterns of multimorbidity, rather than individual diseases alone, could help make prevention more personalized.

medical.title: Starting social media younger linked to anxiety and depression in teens
medical.summary: The age at which adolescents first start using social media may be more important to their mental health than whether they have a social media account at all, new UNSW Sydney research suggests.

medical.title: How cannabis legalization affects substance use
medical.summary: The legalization of cannabis affects substance use, with the potential for both negative and positive effects on public health, a new McGill-led study found.

medical.title: Movement reveals shared visual coding rules in mouse and monkey brains
medical.summary: Seeing and moving are directly linked in the brain. When we stand still, the visual scene barely shifts. When we run, by contrast, the environment rushes past, so the signals reaching the eye become more variable and change faster. Because animals generate this movement themselves, the change is predictable, and the brain can adjust at the moment movement starts rather than waiting for new visual input.

medical.title: What survivors and caregivers should know about stroke rehab
medical.summary: Every year, hundreds of thousands of people in the U.S. live through a stroke. Survivors may face challenges with walking, eating, speaking and other essential parts of life.

medical.title: Each breath is linked to brain activity, offering clues to epilepsy-related breathing failures
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of California San Diego shows that the brain does not simply respond to breathing as a steady rhythm. Instead, the detailed shape of each individual breath is closely linked to the shape of neural activity in brain regions involved in cognition, emotion and memory.

science.title: Industrial-scale microbial foods—growth strategies for the next-generation protein market
science.summary: The question is no longer whether microbial foods can be made. The question now is who can be first to turn them into an industry. KAIST researchers have analyzed the conditions required for the microbial food industry to succeed across manufacturing, markets and regulation, and have proposed growth strategies for the next-generation protein industry.

science.title: A Permian fossil may reveal the oldest known flowering-plant structure
science.summary: Despite the importance and dominance of angiosperms ("flowering plants") in the current ecosystem, it is rather surprising that we know so little about their origin and early evolution. Paleobotanists have been making efforts to decipher these enigmas. Unfortunately, their efforts are characterized by an "unbroken record of failure," as Tom Harris put it.

science.title: Farm-based nanopore sequencing study reports reliable genetic testing results
science.summary: Fast, on-farm genetic testing for cattle is practical and achievable for northern producers, according to University of Queensland research. In partnership with Meat & Livestock Australia and the Department of Primary Industries, a team from UQ's Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation (QAAFI) tested low-pass nanopore sequencing on three commercial farms. Associate Professor Elizabeth Ross said the team produced reliable data for age, genomic breeding values (GBVs) and parentage for about 24 animals in less than 24 hours on each farm.

science.title: New method swaps single atom in a molecule to speed drug discovery
science.summary: Swapping out one letter in a word can entirely change its meaning. Similarly, swapping one atom in a molecule can completely change its identity. A group of chemists at the University of Chicago has demonstrated a new way to make a single-atom edit to a molecule without changing any of its other components. The innovative method can be used to make a family of molecules known as pyrroles, including many widely used medicines, and is significantly simpler, faster and more cost-effective than previous processes.

science.title: No smartphone, no problem: Plants have their own built-in 'Season-Meter'
science.summary: You may check your phone before deciding what to wear tomorrow. Plants do something similar: they carry an internal gadget called a "Season-Meter" that tracks temperatures over the preceding weeks or months to help determine when to flower. By comparing two wild perennial plant species over two years, researchers from the University of Tsukuba found that each of the three genes in this Season-Meter operates over a different timescale, ranging from days to nearly five months, and that together they reliably forecast all four seasons of the year. The research is published in PLOS One.

science.title: Small-plane fuel raises lead levels up to sevenfold near Oregon airports, study suggests
science.summary: Emissions from aircraft that use leaded aviation gasoline are a significant source of environmental pollution in neighborhoods near regional airports, according to a new study by researchers at Oregon State University and Portland State University. The findings were published in Communications Sustainability.

science.title: September 2026 Satellite Puzzler
science.summary: Here’s the August 2026 puzzler. Quick, where is this? And what makes this place interesting or unique?

science.title: Why atmospheric nanoparticles grow at similar rates everywhere
science.summary: Aerosols have a profound influence on air quality, human health, clouds and climate, but new particle formation in the atmosphere has remained a scientific conundrum. Large fractions of airborne fine particulate matter consist of secondary organic aerosols (SOA) formed by gas-to-particle conversion of organic precursor molecules in the atmosphere. The growth rates of these atmospheric nanoparticles, however, have remained enigmatic: They are often smaller and less dependent on condensable vapor concentration than expected.

science.title: Why do some proteins accumulate even on protein-resistant surfaces?
science.summary: Proteins with exposed arginine can selectively accumulate even on protein-resistant coatings, as reported by researchers from Science Tokyo. Through an in-depth analysis of which proteins adhere and how they adhere to various anti-fouling surfaces, the team found that arginine disrupts the protective water layer that normally blocks adsorption. Their results will help scientists develop safer and more effective biocompatible materials for medical devices, such as stents and advanced biosensors.

science.title: Why some AI ads fail while others succeed
science.summary: Artificial intelligence can create realistic depictions of just about anything, but that does not mean advertisers should lean on the technology, according to a study led by University of Mississippi professors.

science.title: Four 'Little Red Dot' pairs hint at black hole mergers in early universe
science.summary: After analyzing infrared images captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), an international team of researchers has discovered multiple massive black holes from approximately 12.5–12.8 billion years ago that were actively accumulating surrounding matter and growing rapidly. Some were even on the path to merging, according to a study published Aug. 31 in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan.

science.title: Peptides can form well-defined structures in harsh, Venus-like conditions
science.summary: When exploring solar system bodies for signs of past or present life, scientists have mainly focused on planets that have (or had) a liquid surface similar to Earth's. However, mounting evidence suggests that the ingredients for life may exist in a very different environment: the highly acidic clouds that blanket Venus.

science.title: Loss of kelp forests reverberates down to the microbial level
science.summary: As one moves north, Maine's kelp forests are being overtaken by dense mats of carpet-like turf algae. The steady decline of kelp and transition into this new state are altering the ecosystem all the way down to the microbial level, according to a new study in PNAS from Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences.

science.title: A 112°C test may separate 1,000-year-old pottery from recent forgeries
science.summary: Museums around the world now have a new tool to distinguish real ancient clay artifacts from fakes. The research team at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography, led by postdoctoral scholar Yoav Vaknin, found a way to distinguish the magnetism that clay materials acquire over time from the magnetism they acquired the day they were made.

science.title: Scientists put algae to work making fuel. AI reveals which cells are pulling their weight
science.summary: Algae have a habit of turning up where they're not wanted. They coat your swimming pool in green gunk, cling to rocks at the beach and even make headlines when they take over prominent reservoirs, such as the White House Reflection Pool. But put them to work in the right setting, and algae can be surprisingly useful. In fact, these plant-like organisms may hold the key to sustainable fuels of the future.

science.title: Researchers make non-recyclable flame-retardant EV composites recyclable
science.summary: Korean researchers have developed a recyclable flame-retardant composite that overcomes a fundamental limitation of conventional flame-retardant composites, which cannot be recycled once cured, while maintaining excellent flame resistance.

science.title: Using AI to track bird migration
science.summary: On hearing the first cuckoo of spring, the poet's heart might sing, and while one swallow does not make a summer, the annual migrations of bird species across continents have fascinated us for centuries. Today, however, technology is giving ornithologists the means to follow these incredible journeys in ways that would have been unimaginable to earlier generations of naturalists.

science.title: Smoky off-flavors in cocoa aren't caused solely by smoke
science.summary: Fermented cocoa occasionally exhibits off-flavors that can compromise the quality of chocolate and other cocoa products. But what causes these undesirable flavors? Researchers at the Leibniz Institute for Food Systems Biology at the Technical University of Munich have now shown that overfermentation of cocoa beans can cause smoky, leathery and cheesy off-flavors. Smoky flavors, therefore, are not necessarily attributable to smoke contamination.

science.title: Malaysia's Sarawak eyes cloud seeding as haze worsens
science.summary: Malaysia's Sarawak state plans cloud-seeding operations in early September, officials said Monday, as smoke from fires in neighboring Indonesia pushes air quality to hazardous levels.

science.title: Plant hormones may offer a way to balance crop yield and disease resistance
science.summary: Growth or immune response? Higher organisms must constantly balance these two priorities. As in humans, hormones regulate this balance in plants. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) have discovered a mechanism by which plant steroid hormones can inhibit immune responses and thereby make resources available for growth.

science.title: An anomalous return of the Odden ice tongue suggests unusual Arctic conditions
science.summary: Data from many sources, including NASA, have shown a significant decrease in Arctic sea ice since 1979. However, the processes driving the melting and freezing of sea ice are complex, and fluctuations occur throughout the year. Short-term variations in temperature, winds, ocean convection and water salinity within a certain region can also affect how much ice can reform or melt.

science.title: Dispelling six myths about back‑to‑school readiness
science.summary: August always feels like one long Sunday to me. It is also a time of year when parents across Canada begin the ritual of preparing their children for September.

environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

environment.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. environment.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
environment.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Adenotonsillectomy tied to increase in respiratory tract infections in children
mix_items.summary: Adenotonsillectomy (ATE) is associated with increased odds of hospital visits due to upper and lower respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in children, according to a study published online July 31 in the Journal of Rhinology.

mix_items.title: Higher vitamin B12 levels in both parents associated with a lower risk of birth defects
mix_items.summary: A prospective cohort study quantifying the associations of parental vitamin B12 and red blood cell (RBC) folate with birth defects found that higher parental vitamin B12 before conception and higher maternal RBC folate concentrations after conception were associated with lower birth defect risk.

mix_items.title: Industrial-scale microbial foods—growth strategies for the next-generation protein market
mix_items.summary: The question is no longer whether microbial foods can be made. The question now is who can be first to turn them into an industry. KAIST researchers have analyzed the conditions required for the microbial food industry to succeed across manufacturing, markets and regulation, and have proposed growth strategies for the next-generation protein industry.

mix_items.title: A Permian fossil may reveal the oldest known flowering-plant structure
mix_items.summary: Despite the importance and dominance of angiosperms ("flowering plants") in the current ecosystem, it is rather surprising that we know so little about their origin and early evolution. Paleobotanists have been making efforts to decipher these enigmas. Unfortunately, their efforts are characterized by an "unbroken record of failure," as Tom Harris put it.

mix_items.title: Farm-based nanopore sequencing study reports reliable genetic testing results
mix_items.summary: Fast, on-farm genetic testing for cattle is practical and achievable for northern producers, according to University of Queensland research. In partnership with Meat & Livestock Australia and the Department of Primary Industries, a team from UQ's Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation (QAAFI) tested low-pass nanopore sequencing on three commercial farms. Associate Professor Elizabeth Ross said the team produced reliable data for age, genomic breeding values (GBVs) and parentage for about 24 animals in less than 24 hours on each farm.

mix_items.title: New method swaps single atom in a molecule to speed drug discovery
mix_items.summary: Swapping out one letter in a word can entirely change its meaning. Similarly, swapping one atom in a molecule can completely change its identity. A group of chemists at the University of Chicago has demonstrated a new way to make a single-atom edit to a molecule without changing any of its other components. The innovative method can be used to make a family of molecules known as pyrroles, including many widely used medicines, and is significantly simpler, faster and more cost-effective than previous processes.

mix_items.title: Estimated glucose disposal rate inversely linked to benign prostatic hyperplasia
mix_items.summary: There is a negative link between estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men, according to a study published online Aug. 25 in The Aging Male.

mix_items.title: Lab-grown nerves match human sensory signal speeds, enabling tests of myelin repair
mix_items.summary: Rice University and collaborators in Switzerland have developed a platform to grow human-derived nerve cells and Schwann cells, supporting cells that form a protective coating called myelin around nerve fibers. This platform enables the formation of functional myelin in a three-dimensional, lab-grown environment. Researchers confirmed that it worked by measuring an increase in the speed of electrical signals traveling across networks of connected nerve cells.

mix_items.title: No smartphone, no problem: Plants have their own built-in 'Season-Meter'
mix_items.summary: You may check your phone before deciding what to wear tomorrow. Plants do something similar: they carry an internal gadget called a "Season-Meter" that tracks temperatures over the preceding weeks or months to help determine when to flower. By comparing two wild perennial plant species over two years, researchers from the University of Tsukuba found that each of the three genes in this Season-Meter operates over a different timescale, ranging from days to nearly five months, and that together they reliably forecast all four seasons of the year. The research is published in PLOS One.

mix_items.title: Semen facilitates infection with mpox virus, study shows
mix_items.summary: The mpox virus used to be transmitted predominantly from animals to humans. In recent years, however, new virus variants have become increasingly capable of spreading from person to person. Researchers at Goethe University and Universitätsmedizin Frankfurt have now found that seminal fluid facilitates the uptake of the mpox virus into cells. Their study is published in the journal Emerging Microbes & Infections.

mix_items.title: Updated guideline issued on migraine prevention medications for adults
mix_items.summary: To help clinicians determine which medications may be most effective at preventing migraine in adults, the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and American Headache Society (AHS) have issued a joint practice guideline update with evidence-based recommendations, published in Neurology, and Headache. This update to the AAN and AHS 2012 guideline is endorsed by the American Academy of Family Physicians.

mix_items.title: Tumor 'floor plans' may predict immunotherapy response better than current biomarkers
mix_items.summary: Spatial transcriptomics is a powerful tool for creating a detailed map of not just how genes are expressed in a piece of tissue, but also where genetic activity takes place in different cells and locations within the tissue. This is especially valuable for studying tumors, which each have their own unique microenvironment that affects how they behave.

mix_items.title: Small-plane fuel raises lead levels up to sevenfold near Oregon airports, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Emissions from aircraft that use leaded aviation gasoline are a significant source of environmental pollution in neighborhoods near regional airports, according to a new study by researchers at Oregon State University and Portland State University. The findings were published in Communications Sustainability.

mix_items.title: September 2026 Satellite Puzzler
mix_items.summary: Here’s the August 2026 puzzler. Quick, where is this? And what makes this place interesting or unique?

mix_items.title: 2011 to 2021 saw heart failure-related hospitalization rise in CKD
mix_items.summary: For patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), rates of heart failure-related hospitalization increased from 2011 to 2021, according to a study published in the September issue of Kidney International Reports.

mix_items.title: Damaged red blood cells can trigger inflammation
mix_items.summary: When red blood cells break down, they release heme, a component of hemoglobin that can contribute to inflammation and damage tissues and blood vessels. Researchers at Lund University have identified a mechanism by which heme activates an inflammatory reaction in the blood. They also were able to block this pathway in experimental models. The findings could have implications for diseases and conditions involving extensive breakdown of red blood cells, including hemolytic uremic syndrome and malaria.

mix_items.title: Why atmospheric nanoparticles grow at similar rates everywhere
mix_items.summary: Aerosols have a profound influence on air quality, human health, clouds and climate, but new particle formation in the atmosphere has remained a scientific conundrum. Large fractions of airborne fine particulate matter consist of secondary organic aerosols (SOA) formed by gas-to-particle conversion of organic precursor molecules in the atmosphere. The growth rates of these atmospheric nanoparticles, however, have remained enigmatic: They are often smaller and less dependent on condensable vapor concentration than expected.

mix_items.title: New AI method can support real-time management of infectious diseases
mix_items.summary: For the past 25 years, one discipline has been revolutionizing epidemiology: phylodynamics. By using genetic sequences, scientists can study how pathogens evolve. Thanks to mathematics, these data can be coherently organized into phylogenetic trees, with each branch representing a chain of transmission and each leaf representing an individual infection.

mix_items.title: Why do some proteins accumulate even on protein-resistant surfaces?
mix_items.summary: Proteins with exposed arginine can selectively accumulate even on protein-resistant coatings, as reported by researchers from Science Tokyo. Through an in-depth analysis of which proteins adhere and how they adhere to various anti-fouling surfaces, the team found that arginine disrupts the protective water layer that normally blocks adsorption. Their results will help scientists develop safer and more effective biocompatible materials for medical devices, such as stents and advanced biosensors.

mix_items.title: Health systems joining efforts to reduce homelessness
mix_items.summary: From developing housing to deploying mobile medical units, most of the nation's large health systems are investing in efforts to alleviate homelessness—and, in turn, reduce emergency care costs, new Cornell research finds.

mix_items.title: Why some AI ads fail while others succeed
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence can create realistic depictions of just about anything, but that does not mean advertisers should lean on the technology, according to a study led by University of Mississippi professors.

mix_items.title: Four 'Little Red Dot' pairs hint at black hole mergers in early universe
mix_items.summary: After analyzing infrared images captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), an international team of researchers has discovered multiple massive black holes from approximately 12.5–12.8 billion years ago that were actively accumulating surrounding matter and growing rapidly. Some were even on the path to merging, according to a study published Aug. 31 in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan.

mix_items.title: Long-term intensive blood-pressure control reduces dementia risk, community-led trial finds
mix_items.summary: In a community-based trial in rural China, an intensive blood pressure-lowering intervention reduced the incidence of dementia compared with usual care, according to results from the China Rural Hypertension Control Program presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

mix_items.title: Peptides can form well-defined structures in harsh, Venus-like conditions
mix_items.summary: When exploring solar system bodies for signs of past or present life, scientists have mainly focused on planets that have (or had) a liquid surface similar to Earth's. However, mounting evidence suggests that the ingredients for life may exist in a very different environment: the highly acidic clouds that blanket Venus.

mix_items.title: Loss of kelp forests reverberates down to the microbial level
mix_items.summary: As one moves north, Maine's kelp forests are being overtaken by dense mats of carpet-like turf algae. The steady decline of kelp and transition into this new state are altering the ecosystem all the way down to the microbial level, according to a new study in PNAS from Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences.

mix_items.title: A 112°C test may separate 1,000-year-old pottery from recent forgeries
mix_items.summary: Museums around the world now have a new tool to distinguish real ancient clay artifacts from fakes. The research team at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography, led by postdoctoral scholar Yoav Vaknin, found a way to distinguish the magnetism that clay materials acquire over time from the magnetism they acquired the day they were made.

mix_items.title: Scientists put algae to work making fuel. AI reveals which cells are pulling their weight
mix_items.summary: Algae have a habit of turning up where they're not wanted. They coat your swimming pool in green gunk, cling to rocks at the beach and even make headlines when they take over prominent reservoirs, such as the White House Reflection Pool. But put them to work in the right setting, and algae can be surprisingly useful. In fact, these plant-like organisms may hold the key to sustainable fuels of the future.

mix_items.title: Poor diet may worsen genetic causes of male infertility, study finds
mix_items.summary: Lifestyle factors can worsen the effects of genetic causes of male infertility, finds new research that could help explain why men carrying similar genetic mutations often experience different levels of fertility impairment.

mix_items.title: Researchers make non-recyclable flame-retardant EV composites recyclable
mix_items.summary: Korean researchers have developed a recyclable flame-retardant composite that overcomes a fundamental limitation of conventional flame-retardant composites, which cannot be recycled once cured, while maintaining excellent flame resistance.

mix_items.title: Evidence often falls short in neuroscience reports of sex-dependent effects, analysis finds
mix_items.summary: Studies in the behavioral and brain sciences reporting a major sex-dependent effect—that a drug, treatment or other intervention is more effective in one sex than another—are supported by appropriate evidence less than 25% of the time, an analysis finds.

mix_items.title: Mouth ulcers: Why have I got them and how can I get rid of them?
mix_items.summary: If you've ever had a mouth ulcer, you'll know how much a tiny sore can take over your day. These small, painful patches that suddenly appear inside your mouth make eating, drinking and even talking surprisingly uncomfortable.

mix_items.title: TAVI-first strategy noninferior to a PCI-first strategy in patients with severe aortic stenosis and concomitant CAD
mix_items.summary: A TAVI-first strategy was noninferior to a PCI-first strategy after one year's follow-up, according to results presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Four disease profiles reveal uneven benefits from lifestyle programs after age 70
mix_items.summary: Older adults living with several chronic diseases, a condition known as multimorbidity, may respond differently to interventions aimed at preventing disability, depending on the combination of diseases they have. A new study, published in Nature Aging and led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Rome, suggests that looking at patterns of multimorbidity, rather than individual diseases alone, could help make prevention more personalized.

mix_items.title: Using AI to track bird migration
mix_items.summary: On hearing the first cuckoo of spring, the poet's heart might sing, and while one swallow does not make a summer, the annual migrations of bird species across continents have fascinated us for centuries. Today, however, technology is giving ornithologists the means to follow these incredible journeys in ways that would have been unimaginable to earlier generations of naturalists.

mix_items.title: Smoky off-flavors in cocoa aren't caused solely by smoke
mix_items.summary: Fermented cocoa occasionally exhibits off-flavors that can compromise the quality of chocolate and other cocoa products. But what causes these undesirable flavors? Researchers at the Leibniz Institute for Food Systems Biology at the Technical University of Munich have now shown that overfermentation of cocoa beans can cause smoky, leathery and cheesy off-flavors. Smoky flavors, therefore, are not necessarily attributable to smoke contamination.

mix_items.title: Malaysia's Sarawak eyes cloud seeding as haze worsens
mix_items.summary: Malaysia's Sarawak state plans cloud-seeding operations in early September, officials said Monday, as smoke from fires in neighboring Indonesia pushes air quality to hazardous levels.

mix_items.title: Plant hormones may offer a way to balance crop yield and disease resistance
mix_items.summary: Growth or immune response? Higher organisms must constantly balance these two priorities. As in humans, hormones regulate this balance in plants. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) have discovered a mechanism by which plant steroid hormones can inhibit immune responses and thereby make resources available for growth.

mix_items.title: Starting social media younger linked to anxiety and depression in teens
mix_items.summary: The age at which adolescents first start using social media may be more important to their mental health than whether they have a social media account at all, new UNSW Sydney research suggests.

mix_items.title: How cannabis legalization affects substance use
mix_items.summary: The legalization of cannabis affects substance use, with the potential for both negative and positive effects on public health, a new McGill-led study found.

mix_items.title: An anomalous return of the Odden ice tongue suggests unusual Arctic conditions
mix_items.summary: Data from many sources, including NASA, have shown a significant decrease in Arctic sea ice since 1979. However, the processes driving the melting and freezing of sea ice are complex, and fluctuations occur throughout the year. Short-term variations in temperature, winds, ocean convection and water salinity within a certain region can also affect how much ice can reform or melt.

mix_items.title: Dispelling six myths about back‑to‑school readiness
mix_items.summary: August always feels like one long Sunday to me. It is also a time of year when parents across Canada begin the ritual of preparing their children for September.

mix_items.title: Movement reveals shared visual coding rules in mouse and monkey brains
mix_items.summary: Seeing and moving are directly linked in the brain. When we stand still, the visual scene barely shifts. When we run, by contrast, the environment rushes past, so the signals reaching the eye become more variable and change faster. Because animals generate this movement themselves, the change is predictable, and the brain can adjust at the moment movement starts rather than waiting for new visual input.

mix_items.title: What survivors and caregivers should know about stroke rehab
mix_items.summary: Every year, hundreds of thousands of people in the U.S. live through a stroke. Survivors may face challenges with walking, eating, speaking and other essential parts of life.

mix_items.title: Each breath is linked to brain activity, offering clues to epilepsy-related breathing failures
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of California San Diego shows that the brain does not simply respond to breathing as a steady rhythm. Instead, the detailed shape of each individual breath is closely linked to the shape of neural activity in brain regions involved in cognition, emotion and memory.

mix_items.title: Gold miners breach a crucial refuge for rescued Sumatran orangutans
mix_items.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

mix_items.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: Recording a rainforest before Indonesia’s new capital changes it
mix_items.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

joke_ro.text: Mi-am pus viata in ordine. Acum nu mai gasesc nimic.

satire_ro.title: Messi, la retragerea de la Națională: „Marele meu regret este că n-am fost antrenat de Gigi Becali!”
